title: How Our Solar System Began
summary: Travel back about 4.6 billion years to watch the Sun and planets form from a cloud of gas and dust. Then explore all eight planets, meet some of their natural satellites, and finish with a short quiz.

steps.text: About four point six billion years ago, there was no Earth or Sun here, just a huge cloud of gas and dust. These three models show stages of its story. Start with the wide, wispy cloud on the left.
Gravity is a pull between things that have mass. It pulled the cloud's gas and dust closer together. The inward arrows beside this smaller cloud show the direction of that pull.
As the cloud shrank, it spun faster, like a spinning skater pulling in their arms. Compare the slowly moving dust in the wide cloud with the faster dust in the smaller cloud.
Most of the material gathered in the center, where it became more crowded and hotter. This center grew into a young star: our Sun. The glowing model shows that later stage, not a solid ball of rock.

Around the young Sun, leftover gas and dust formed a spinning, flattened disc. From this higher viewpoint, notice how thin it is. This material would help build the planets; the bright circles only mark paths.

Follow the story from the wide cloud to the smaller spinning cloud, then to the young Sun and its disc. Real changes took millions of years. Our motion is sped up, and these models' sizes and distances are not to scale.

scenes.title: A Star and Its Planet Builders

nodes.label: Simplified sizes, distances, motion and stages

steps.text: The young Sun's center became hot enough for fusion. Tiny particles joined and released energy, making the Sun shine. The glowing model beside it shows the center; all sizes, distances, motion and stages here are simplified.
The Sun is a star made mostly of hydrogen and helium. It holds almost all the mass in our Solar System. Fusion deep inside supplies its light and heat.

In the surrounding disc, some dust grains stuck together. Read this magnified row from tiny grains to a pebble, a boulder and a growing world. Over a very long time, collisions helped some clumps join and grow.
Near the hot young Sun, rock and metal could stay solid, but ice could not. These materials helped build the four rocky inner planets. The warm-colored zone marks their part of the disc.
Farther out, it was colder, so ice could join rock in growing worlds. Some large worlds gathered lots of gas. The outer planets developed in this colder region; Jupiter became the largest planet.

The young Sun helped clear leftover gas. Asteroids and icy comets remained alongside eight planets. The Sun's gravity pulls planets inward, while their forward motion keeps them traveling around it instead of falling straight in.

nodes.label: Back row: relative planet sizes; distances compressed
Front row: enlarged copies for inspection

steps.text: Nearest the Sun come Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. All four have rocky surfaces. The back row compares their actual relative sizes. Their distances are compressed, the Sun is shrunk, and the front copies are enlarged for inspection.

Inspect Mercury's cratered ground as it turns. Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. With almost no atmosphere to hold heat, its ground gets very hot in sunlight and very cold during its long nights.

Venus is almost Earth's size, but its rocky ground is hidden beneath thick clouds. Its thick atmosphere traps heat like a heavy blanket. That makes Venus the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Watch Earth's continents and blue oceans turn into view. Earth has liquid-water oceans and an atmosphere that helps support life. It is the only world where we know life exists.

Mars looks reddish because some surface minerals contain rusty iron. Look for its long canyon and broad volcanic rise as it turns. Mars has huge volcanoes, deep canyons, and signs that liquid water flowed there long ago.

Compare the back row again: tiny Mercury, nearly equal Venus and Earth, then smaller Mars. These planets grew from similar rocky building materials. Their distances from the Sun and their atmospheres helped them become very different worlds.

nodes.label: Exhibit sizes and separations are compressed
Eight planets: compressed sizes and distances

steps.text: Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt, with many rocky objects and enormous empty spaces between them. It is not a crowded wall. Our exhibit compresses distances and changes sizes so we can explore.

Jupiter is the largest planet, about eleven Earths wide. The little Earth beside it shows that size difference. Jupiter is a gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and its Great Red Spot is a huge storm.
Saturn is another gas giant, made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Its bright rings contain countless separate pieces of ice and some rocky material, rather than one solid sheet.
Watch the rings narrow as we move toward their edge. Saturn's rings are extremely thin compared with their width, like an enormous, delicate disc.
Uranus is an ice giant, and it spins almost on its side. Deep inside are water, ammonia, and methane under great pressure. The name ice giant does not mean it is a giant snowball.
Neptune is also an ice giant and is the farthest planet from the Sun. Powerful winds race through its atmosphere. Methane helps give both Neptune and Uranus their blue-green colors.

Look down at all eight planets circling the Sun. From nearest to farthest, their order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. These sizes, distances, and speeds are changed for our model.

The outer planets grew in the colder part of the young Solar System, where icy material could help build large cores. Jupiter and Saturn gathered especially huge amounts of gas. Uranus and Neptune became the ice giants.

A scientific explanation supported by evidence
Gas and dust → Sun and planets → worlds with moons

steps.text: A natural satellite is a naturally formed object orbiting another body. A planet's satellites are called moons. Watch Earth's Moon circle Earth. Planets orbit the Sun. Our display simplifies sizes, distances, and speeds.
Earth has one Moon. This small reconstruction shows the leading explanation: a large body struck the young Earth. Debris gathered together in orbit and formed the Moon.

sfx.prompt: deep muffled impact followed by brief debris rumble

steps.text: Mercury and Venus have no moons. Mars has two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos. Follow their separate paths around Mars. The four giant planets each have many moons.
Jupiter's moon Europa has an icy surface crossed by cracks. Scientists have strong evidence for an ocean beneath that ice. The ocean is hidden below the surface, not visible here.
Saturn's moon Titan wears a thick, hazy atmosphere. Beneath the haze are lakes of liquid methane and ethane, not water. A moon can be a surprisingly different world!

Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune all have many moons. Some moons grew from material around young planets. Others were captured by gravity. Moons travel with their planets as the planets orbit the Sun.
Which is hotter, Mercury or Venus? It is Venus: its thick atmosphere traps heat. Our Solar System began as a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity gathered material into the Sun and planets.
What does Earth's Moon orbit, Earth or Mars? Earth! We have followed a cloud becoming a star, planets, and worlds with moons. Now choose what our Solar System formed from.

quiz.question: What did our Solar System form from?

options.label: A cloud of gas and dust

correct.text: Correct! Gravity gathered a cloud of gas and dust into the Sun and planets.
